text: Can you find me a practice problem from the stewart calculus book?

Evaluate the limit, if it exists:

$$\lim_{x \to -3} \frac{x^2 - 9}{x^2 + x - 6}$$

Show each step, and say why you're allowed to do it.
title: Problem 1 (written in the style of Stewart §2.3, not taken from the book)

text:
Before we start, a reminder: anything you share here, including notes I read, is sent to Anthropic's API, which is a third party.

I couldn't get a problem out of the book. Stewart §2.3, Calculating Limits Using the Limit Laws, is the section for what you practised last time (0/0 limits by factoring). The book tools gave an error three times on that section, once when I tried to read the text and twice when I tried to pull its exercises. So I wrote a problem in the same style instead. **It's mine, not Stewart's**, and it's in your log as Problem 1:

$$\lim_{x \to -3} \frac{x^2 - 9}{x^2 + x - 6}$$

Work it on paper and send me your answer and your steps. Before you factor anything, check what you get if you just plug in $x = -3$. If you get stuck, ask for a hint and I'll give you a nudge, not the answer.

If you'd rather have a real Stewart exercise, we can try the book again later.
